pathway.title: JavaScript Programming
pathway.description: Learn to design, build, test and explain JavaScript applications from fundamentals through professional engineering practice.

course.title: JavaScript Programming — Advanced
course.short_description: An advanced JavaScript course covering runtime internals, prototypes, event-loop semantics, resilient asynchronous design, functional programming, modules, browser APIs, network security, testing, performance and professional application engineering.
course.prerequisites: Completion of JavaScript Programming — Intermediate or equivalent experience with functions, closures, objects, arrays, ES modules, promises, async/await, error handling and Node.js 20+.
learning_outcomes: Explain JavaScript execution, lexical environments, closures, prototypes and memory reachability.
Design resilient asynchronous workflows using promises, cancellation, bounded concurrency and appropriate workers.
Build modular browser applications using safe DOM patterns, browser storage and network APIs.
Apply testing, debugging, performance profiling and maintainable architecture practices.
Identify common JavaScript security risks and implement appropriate client and server boundary controls.
course.dependencies: Node.js 20+ built-ins only; no third-party packages required.

modules.title: Understand the JavaScript runtime and language model
modules.description: Trace execution, scope, closures, object identity, prototypes, and memory behavior.

topics.title: Execution contexts, call stack and JavaScript engines
topics.description: Understand how JavaScript code is prepared and executed, and trace nested calls.

lesson.title: Execution contexts, call stack and JavaScript engines
objectives: Describe the roles of an engine, runtime and host environment.
Trace global and function execution contexts and the call stack.
Explain the limits of the simplified execution model.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: JavaScript source is processed by an engine such as V8, SpiderMonkey or JavaScriptCore. Engines commonly parse source, create internal representations, execute or compile code, and optimize frequently used paths. The exact pipeline differs by engine and version; it is inaccurate to imagine one universal fixed sequence. An execution context is the environment in which a piece of code runs. The global context is established for a script or module, and function calls create function contexts with their own local bindings and control state. The call stack tracks active synchronous calls: a function call places a frame on the stack, and returning removes it. When a function calls another function, the newer call is handled first. This explains ordinary synchronous order and why uncontrolled recursion can overflow the stack. The browser or Node.js host supplies APIs such as timers, file access or networking; those APIs are not all part of the ECMAScript language itself. Keep the distinction between language semantics, engine implementation and host APIs clear when debugging or discussing performance.

topics.title: Lexical environments, closures and this
topics.description: Reason about captured bindings and receiver behavior across function forms.

lesson.title: Lexical environments, closures and this
objectives: Explain lexical scope and closure lifetime.
Compare `this` in ordinary functions and arrow functions.
Use call, apply and bind deliberately.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A lexical environment associates identifiers with bindings and links to an outer environment. Name lookup follows that chain, so a function can access bindings from the place where it was defined. A closure is the combination of a function and the lexical environment it retains access to. This enables factories, callbacks and encapsulated state, but it can also keep large referenced objects reachable longer than intended. JavaScript's `this` is a separate mechanism: for an ordinary function, its value is generally determined by how the function is called, not where it was written. A method call such as `account.read()` supplies `account` as the receiver; extracting the function and calling it alone changes that call form. `call` and `apply` invoke a function with an explicit receiver, while `bind` creates a function with a fixed receiver and optional leading arguments. Arrow functions do not create their own `this`; they capture it lexically from the surrounding scope. That makes arrows useful for callbacks but often unsuitable as object methods when a dynamic receiver is required. Test behavior at the call site instead of guessing from a function's name.

topics.title: Prototypes, classes, descriptors and memory
topics.description: Inspect inheritance and property behavior without treating classes as a separate object system.

lesson.title: Prototypes, classes, descriptors and memory
objectives: Trace property lookup through a prototype chain.
Use classes, inheritance and property descriptors appropriately.
Explain reachability and common memory-retention problems.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: JavaScript objects can delegate property lookup to another object through their internal prototype link. If a property is not an own property, lookup continues along the prototype chain until it is found or the chain ends. `class` syntax provides a clearer notation for constructor functions and prototype-based methods; it does not replace JavaScript's prototype model with classical inheritance in the same sense as some other languages. Prefer composition when it keeps relationships simpler, and avoid deep inheritance chains that make behavior difficult to follow. Property descriptors control attributes such as writability, enumerability and configurability. Getters and setters can expose computed or validated properties, but they should not hide expensive or surprising work. Memory management is based largely on reachability: values that remain reachable from roots such as active stacks and global references cannot be reclaimed. A closure, event listener, cache or detached DOM node can unintentionally retain a large object graph. Garbage collection is automatic, but timing is not under application control. Release listeners, bound caches and references when their owners are finished, and use profiling tools to confirm suspected leaks rather than relying on guesses.

modules.title: Master asynchronous and functional programming
modules.description: Reason about the event loop, promises, concurrency, functional composition, and state.

topics.title: Event loop, tasks, microtasks and Web Workers
topics.description: Predict asynchronous ordering and select the right concurrency mechanism.

lesson.title: Event loop, tasks, microtasks and Web Workers
objectives: Explain the event loop at a conceptual level.
Distinguish microtasks from timer tasks.
Choose workers for CPU-heavy work and promises for asynchronous coordination.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: JavaScript in a typical browser page runs JavaScript on a main thread with a call stack. The host environment coordinates timers, network events, rendering and other work. When the current synchronous stack becomes empty, the event loop can select queued work. Promise reactions and `queueMicrotask` callbacks run as microtasks; timer callbacks are commonly scheduled as tasks (often called macrotasks in teaching material). After a task, the runtime generally drains the microtask queue before proceeding to another task, though rendering and host scheduling details are more nuanced than a single universal diagram. A long synchronous loop blocks the main thread and delays input and rendering. `async`/`await` makes promise-based code easier to read but does not move CPU work to another thread. Web Workers provide separate execution contexts for suitable CPU-intensive work and communicate through messages; they do not directly manipulate the page DOM. Worker startup, serialization or transfer costs mean they are not automatically faster for tiny jobs. In Node.js, worker threads and the event loop have their own host-specific APIs. Always separate concurrency (overlapping progress) from parallelism (simultaneous execution on multiple cores).

topics.title: Promises, async/await and resilient concurrency
topics.description: Compose asynchronous operations and handle cancellation, timeouts and partial failure.

lesson.title: Promises, async/await and resilient concurrency
objectives: Use Promise.all, allSettled, any and race correctly.
Handle rejected promises and cancellation with AbortController.
Bound concurrency and distinguish parallel independent work from dependent steps.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A promise represents an eventual fulfillment value or rejection reason. `then` returns a new promise, so transformations and failures form a chain; returning a promise from a handler adopts its eventual state. `async` functions always return promises, and `await` pauses only that async function's continuation. Start independent operations before awaiting them together when overlap is useful; awaiting each one inside a loop can accidentally serialize work. `Promise.all` fulfills when every input fulfills and rejects as soon as one rejects, but it does not automatically cancel the remaining operations. `Promise.allSettled` reports every outcome, `Promise.any` fulfills with the first fulfillment, and `Promise.race` settles with the first settled outcome. These have different contracts and should not be interchangeable by habit. `AbortController` communicates cancellation to APIs that support its signal, such as fetch; it cannot forcibly stop arbitrary JavaScript computation. For many items, use a concurrency limit to avoid overwhelming a server or exhausting resources. Add timeouts thoughtfully and ensure errors are observed at a layer able to recover, retry safely or explain failure.

topics.title: Functional composition, immutability and performance patterns
topics.description: Compose reusable transformations and reason about memoization and recursion.

lesson.title: Functional composition, immutability and performance patterns
objectives: Use composition and higher-order functions to build pipelines.
Apply immutability without unnecessary copying.
Evaluate memoization and recursion trade-offs.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Functional programming emphasizes transformations, explicit inputs and outputs, and controlled side effects. Function composition connects small functions so the output of one becomes the input of another; this can make pipelines readable when each function has one clear responsibility. Higher-order functions accept or return functions, enabling reusable policies such as sorting rules or validators. Immutability means avoiding unintended changes to shared values. It does not require deep-cloning every object: copy only the structures that change, preserve stable references where appropriate, and understand that spread syntax creates a shallow copy. Memoization caches results for repeated inputs, but it is useful only when the calculation is sufficiently expensive, the key captures all relevant inputs, and the cache has a reasonable lifetime and size. Recursive solutions can be elegant for tree-shaped data, but deep recursion risks stack limits; iterative traversal may be safer for unbounded input. JavaScript's modern array methods include non-mutating alternatives such as `toSorted` in current runtimes, but compatibility requirements must be checked. Measure performance before introducing clever abstractions or caches.

modules.title: Build robust browser and modular applications
modules.description: Design module boundaries, communicate with browser and network APIs, and handle failure safely.

topics.title: ES modules, dynamic imports and application architecture
topics.description: Organize code into explicit boundaries and load optional features on demand.

lesson.title: ES modules, dynamic imports and application architecture
objectives: Use named and default exports with clear module contracts.
Explain static imports, dynamic imports and code splitting.
Apply dependency direction and composition over unnecessary coupling.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: ES modules define file-level boundaries with explicit imports and exports. Named exports make a module's public surface visible and allow multiple related values; a default export can represent one primary value but should not be used automatically for every file. Static imports are resolved before module evaluation and make dependencies discoverable to tools. Dynamic `import()` returns a promise and can load optional code when a feature is needed, which bundlers may use as a code-splitting boundary. Module architecture should keep domain rules independent from presentation and infrastructure where possible. A UI component can depend on a service interface; the domain should not need to know which browser storage implementation or HTTP library is selected. Avoid circular dependencies because they complicate initialization and reasoning. Package managers and lockfiles make dependencies reproducible, but they do not guarantee that a dependency is trustworthy or secure. Review package provenance, maintenance, license and advisories. Keep public module APIs small, document side effects, and test modules through observable contracts rather than internal implementation details.

topics.title: Browser APIs, DOM events and client-side storage
topics.description: Use browser event models and storage APIs with clear security and lifecycle boundaries.

lesson.title: Browser APIs, DOM events and client-side storage
objectives: Explain event capture, target and bubbling phases.
Use event delegation and clean up listeners.
Choose localStorage, sessionStorage or IndexedDB based on data needs.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A DOM event travels through a propagation model that includes capture, target and bubbling phases. Event delegation attaches a listener to a stable ancestor and inspects the event target, which can handle many dynamic child elements without installing one listener per child. Delegation must validate the target carefully and account for nested elements. Listeners should be removed or tied to an owner lifecycle when no longer needed, especially when callbacks close over large objects. `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` are synchronous string stores and should not be used for large datasets or sensitive secrets. IndexedDB is an asynchronous browser database better suited to structured client-side data and larger offline datasets, but it still needs schema/version management and a privacy policy. Browser storage is not automatically trusted: same-origin scripts may access it, and an XSS flaw can expose data. Never store session secrets or sensitive learner information casually. The DOM is a host API; a Worker cannot directly manipulate a page's DOM. Use feature detection and handle storage failures, quota limits, private browsing restrictions and user-cleared data. Keep browser-specific behavior behind an adapter when domain logic should also run in Node.js tests.

topics.title: HTTP APIs, fetch, WebSockets and cross-origin controls
topics.description: Build reliable network clients and understand browser-origin security boundaries.

lesson.title: HTTP APIs, fetch, WebSockets and cross-origin controls
objectives: Check HTTP status and parse response bodies deliberately.
Use cancellation, timeouts and WebSockets for appropriate workloads.
Explain CORS, same-origin policy and safe request handling.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: `fetch` resolves when an HTTP response is available, including many error statuses such as 404 or 500; it does not reject solely because the server returned an unsuccessful status. Check `response.ok` or the status explicitly before treating a response as successful, and validate the body shape before using it. Network code should define timeout and cancellation behavior, avoid logging tokens or personal data, and distinguish transport errors from HTTP errors and application validation errors. WebSockets provide a persistent, bidirectional connection suited to interactive updates, but they need authentication, authorization, origin checks, message validation, rate limits and reconnect strategy. The same-origin policy restricts how documents and scripts interact across origins. CORS is a server-controlled mechanism that allows selected cross-origin browser requests; it is not authentication and does not protect an API from non-browser clients. Avoid wildcard origins with credentials. Do not put secrets in frontend bundles because users can inspect them. Use HTTPS, appropriate cookie protections or carefully managed tokens, and server-side authorization for every protected action. Treat remote responses as untrusted input even when they come from a familiar service.

modules.title: Engineer secure, tested, high-performance software
modules.description: Test and debug complex systems, optimize performance, apply security controls, and deliver a capstone.

topics.title: Testing strategy, debugging and error architecture
topics.description: Design meaningful tests and trace failures across asynchronous boundaries.

lesson.title: Testing strategy, debugging and error architecture
objectives: Separate unit, integration and end-to-end test responsibilities.
Use deterministic tests for asynchronous behavior.
Design error types and debugging evidence that preserve useful context.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A reliable test strategy uses different levels for different risks. Unit tests check focused behavior in isolation; integration tests verify that components work together across boundaries such as a repository and service; end-to-end tests exercise important user journeys through the running system. Tests should assert observable contracts rather than private implementation details. Asynchronous tests must await the promise being tested or return it to the test runner, otherwise the test may finish before the assertion runs. Avoid arbitrary sleeps when a deterministic signal, controlled promise or fake clock is available. Mock external systems at a boundary, but do not mock every internal function or tests can merely confirm the mock setup. Custom error classes can distinguish validation, authorization, network and persistence failures while preserving causes with the `cause` option. Catch errors only when the current layer can recover, translate them into a useful boundary response, or add context before rethrowing. Debugging should gather a reproducible case, stack trace, relevant timing and sanitized inputs. Never include credentials or personal learner data in logs. Test negative paths, retries, cancellation and partial failure as deliberately as success paths.

topics.title: Performance profiling, algorithms and memory diagnostics
topics.description: Measure real bottlenecks and select optimizations that preserve behavior.

lesson.title: Performance profiling, algorithms and memory diagnostics
objectives: Use profiling and performance marks to locate bottlenecks.
Compare algorithmic complexity and data-structure trade-offs.
Apply debouncing, throttling and memory cleanup appropriately.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Performance work starts with a user-visible problem and measurement, not with clever code. Browser developer tools can profile CPU activity, inspect network waterfalls, measure rendering and reveal retained objects; Node.js provides profiling and performance APIs as well. Big-O notation describes how resource use grows with input size, but constants, data shape and runtime behavior also matter. Replacing a repeated linear search with a Map can improve lookup patterns, while adding a cache may increase memory use and invalidation complexity. Debouncing waits until a burst of events pauses, which is useful for search input; throttling limits how often work runs, which can help scroll or resize handlers. Neither should make required updates disappear. Rendering performance often improves by reducing unnecessary work and large synchronous tasks, not by micro-optimizing syntax. Memory leaks commonly arise from retained listeners, timers, detached DOM nodes or unbounded caches. Take heap snapshots and compare retaining paths. Optimize one measured bottleneck at a time, retain regression tests, and measure again under representative conditions. Never trade correctness, accessibility or security for an unverified benchmark improvement.

topics.title: Secure JavaScript and professional capstone engineering
topics.description: Apply browser and application security principles in a complete, testable system.

lesson.title: Secure JavaScript and professional capstone engineering
objectives: Recognize XSS, injection and unsafe trust boundaries.
Apply safe rendering, validation, authorization and dependency hygiene.
Plan and evaluate a modular capstone application.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: JavaScript security is primarily about controlling trust boundaries. Cross-site scripting occurs when untrusted content is interpreted as executable markup or script; prefer textContent and safe templating, and sanitize only when rich HTML is genuinely required using a maintained, correctly configured sanitizer. Avoid building SQL, shell or HTML commands by concatenating untrusted strings; use parameterized APIs and context-appropriate encoding. Validate input on the server even when the browser also validates it. Authentication establishes identity, while authorization decides whether that identity may perform a particular action; every protected server operation needs authorization checks. HTTPS protects data in transit but does not make a compromised endpoint safe. Content Security Policy can reduce the impact of some script injection paths when deployed carefully, but it is not a substitute for safe coding. Keep dependencies current, review provenance and advisories, minimize permissions and secrets, and never ship private keys in client bundles. A professional capstone should demonstrate architecture, tests, accessibility, error handling, performance evidence and a threat model. Security claims must be supported by implemented controls and tests, not by a checklist alone.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: This runnable example demonstrates secure javascript and professional capstone engineering. Predict its output, run it with Node.js 20+, and change one input to test the behavior contract.

blocks.title: Concept flow
blocks.alt_text: Assigning untrusted content to textContent displays it as text instead of parsing it as HTML.
blocks.content: untrusted string → textContent (text node); avoid string → innerHTML (HTML parser) for untrusted input

blocks.title: Guided practice
instructions: Design a secure mini catalogue client with modular services, validated API responses, safe DOM rendering, tests and a threat model. Include an explanation of server-side authorization and dependency update policy.

A normal case and a boundary or failure case are checked.
The learner can explain the diagram and one limitation.

blocks.title: Secure Real-Time Learning Resource Explorer
blocks.purpose: Design and implement a modular JavaScript application that searches and presents a fictional catalogue, handles asynchronous API responses, supports live update simulation, and demonstrates secure rendering, testing, performance and accessibility practices.
privacy_and_limits: Use invented records only; do not connect to Marian, school systems, real learner data or production services.
Do not place secrets or credentials in browser code or local storage.
A local demonstration is not proof of production security; document controls that require server-side implementation.
requirements: Use ES modules with clear UI, domain and data-service boundaries.
Implement a cancellable fetch client that checks HTTP status, validates response shape and reports typed errors.
Render untrusted text safely and implement accessible search with a debounced input.
Use a Map or another justified data structure for repeated lookups and provide measured performance evidence.
Implement a simulated live-update adapter or WebSocket client with message validation and reconnect limits.
Add unit and integration tests, including rejected requests, malformed data, cancellation and empty results.
Document a threat model covering XSS, authorization, CORS, secrets, dependency risk and logging.
Provide setup instructions, architecture diagrams, accessibility checks and a limitations section.
suggested_steps: Define data contracts, threat model and module dependency diagram.
Implement pure domain transformations and unit tests.
Build the API adapter with cancellation, status checks and response validation.
Create accessible UI rendering with safe text handling and debounced search.
Add live updates, bounded reconnect behavior and deterministic tests.
Profile representative data, optimize only measured bottlenecks and document results.
Complete security review, integration tests, README and final demonstration.
success_checks: All untrusted text is rendered safely and no secrets are embedded in the client.
Network failures, HTTP errors, invalid payloads and cancellation are distinguishable.
Tests cover normal, boundary and failure behavior and pass deterministically.
Module dependencies are understandable and domain logic can be tested outside the browser.
Performance claims include reproducible measurements and no correctness regression.
Threat model clearly separates client controls from server-enforced authorization.

rubric.look_for: Correct event-loop, promise, closure, prototype and execution explanations.
Clear module boundaries, reusable domain logic, explicit contracts and maintainability.
Safe rendering, validated inputs, server authorization awareness, secret hygiene and threat model.
Unit/integration coverage, deterministic async tests, cancellation and error behavior.
Measured optimization, accessible interactions, clear diagrams and reproducible instructions.

revision_notes: Treat all external and user-controlled data as untrusted.
Use safe rendering, server-side validation and per-action authorization.
CSP and HTTPS are defense layers, not substitutes for secure design.

final_assessment.title: JavaScript Programming — Advanced Final Assessment
final_assessment.instructions: Answer twelve multiple-choice questions (4 marks each) and complete both coding tasks (26 marks each). Total: 100 marks. Use invented data and provide deterministic tests.

multiple_choice.prompt: Which statement best describes lexical scope?

choices.text: The caller replaces all outer bindings
Scope is determined by console output
Name lookup follows the function's enclosing lexical environments

multiple_choice.prompt: Where are class prototype methods normally found?

choices.text: As a new own method on each instance

multiple_choice.prompt: What is the key difference between concurrency and parallelism?

choices.text: Concurrency overlaps progress; parallelism executes simultaneously
They are identical in every context

multiple_choice.prompt: Which queue handles promise reactions in the common browser model?
What does Promise.all do when one input rejects?

choices.text: Returns every error as a value
Rejects, without automatically cancelling the other operations

multiple_choice.prompt: What is a risk of a shallow copy?

choices.text: Nested objects may remain shared references
A promise for a module namespace

multiple_choice.prompt: What should a fetch client do with a 404 response?

choices.text: Check response.ok/status and handle the HTTP error explicitly

multiple_choice.prompt: What is event delegation based on?

choices.text: Event propagation to an ancestor listener
Measure and identify a real bottleneck

multiple_choice.prompt: Which API safely inserts a string as text?
Where must authorization for protected operations be enforced?

choices.text: On the server for each protected operation
